question.prompt: Ant Amelia starts on the number line at \(0\) and crawls in the following manner. For \(n=1,\) \(2,\) \(3;\) Amelia chooses a time duration \(t_n\) and an increment \(x_n\) independently and uniformly at random from the interval \((0,1).\) During the \(n\)th step of the process, Amelia moves \(x_n\) units in the positive direction, using up \(t_n\) minutes. If the total elapsed time has exceeded \(1\) minute during the \(n\)th step, she stops at the end of that step; otherwise, she continues with the next step, taking at most \(3\) steps in all. What is the probability that Amelia’s position when she stops will be greater than \(1?\)

solutions.title: Use areas and a volume
solutions.explanation:
Amelia cannot stop after one step because \(t_1<1\). She therefore takes either two or three steps, and this choice depends only on the time variables, independently of all the distances.

The pair \((t_1,t_2)\) is uniformly distributed in a unit square. The line \(t_1+t_2=1\) divides that square into two triangles of equal area. Therefore Amelia stops after two steps with probability \(\tfrac12\), and she takes three steps with probability \(\tfrac12\). The equality case has probability zero.

If she takes two steps, the same unit-square argument gives
\[
\Pr(x_1+x_2>1)=\frac12.
\]
If she takes three steps, consider the uniformly distributed point \((x_1,x_2,x_3)\) in a unit cube. The event \(x_1+x_2+x_3<1\) is the triangular pyramid with vertices
\[
(0,0,0),\quad(1,0,0),\quad(0,1,0),\quad(0,0,1).
\]
Its base in the plane \(x_3=0\) is a right triangle of area \(\tfrac12\), and its height is 1. Its volume is therefore
\[
\frac13\cdot\frac12\cdot1=\frac16.
\]
The cube has volume 1, so
\[
\Pr(x_1+x_2+x_3>1)=1-\frac16=\frac56.
\]
The two stopping cases are disjoint and exhaustive. Since the times and distances are independent, the desired probability is
\[
\frac12\cdot\frac12+\frac12\cdot\frac56
=\frac14+\frac5{12}
=\boxed{\frac23}.
\]
The answer is choice C.

solutions.title: Replace volume with symmetry
solutions.explanation:
The stopping rule gives just two cases. To handle the three-step distance without a solid-volume formula, we can compare three random numbers with their largest one.

First, \(t_1<1\), so Amelia always takes a second step. In the unit square of possible \((t_1,t_2)\), the line \(t_1+t_2=1\) divides the area in half. Thus she takes two steps with probability \(\tfrac12\) and three steps with probability \(\tfrac12\).

The same square argument shows that her two-step distance exceeds 1 with probability \(\tfrac12\).

To find the three-step probability, set
\[
U=x_1,\qquad V=x_2,\qquad W=1-x_3.
\]
These are still three independent uniform numbers in \((0,1)\). Moreover,
\[
x_1+x_2+x_3<1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
U+V<W.
\]
For \(U+V<W\) to hold, \(W\) must be the largest of the three numbers. By symmetry this happens with probability \(\tfrac13\); ties have probability zero.

View \((U,V,W)\) as a uniform point in a unit cube and restrict to the region where \(W\) is largest. A horizontal slice at height \(W=m\), for \(0<m<1\), is the square \(0<U<m\), \(0<V<m\). The diagonal \(U+V=m\) divides this square into two congruent triangles. Specifically, the pairing
\[
(U,V,m)\longmapsto(m-U,m-V,m)
\]
exchanges the triangle \(U+V<m\) with the triangle \(U+V>m\). It matches equal areas at every height, so stacking the slices gives equal volumes for the two portions of the region. Thus, given that \(W\) is largest, exactly half the region satisfies \(U+V<W\). Consequently,
\[
\Pr(U+V<W)=\frac13\cdot\frac12=\frac16.
\]
Thus the three-step distance exceeds 1 with probability \(\tfrac56\). Equality has probability zero.

The step count depends only on the times, independently of the distances. Combining the two stopping cases gives
\[
\frac12\cdot\frac12+\frac12\cdot\frac56
=\boxed{\frac23}.
\]
The answer is choice C.
